_about: Journal insights for Carol's own Unit 1 deck (38 slides). Apply with insights_u01.py. Never run enrich.py on this deck: it deletes everything after the first marker.

entries.label: Direction Failure · the whole before the parts
entries.text: Organisations often let functions, departments and individuals pursue objectives without enough understanding of how those objectives contribute to the larger organisational intent. The result can be excellent local performance without coherent enterprise progress. Start with the whole, then locate each part within it.

entries.label: Influence Failure · symbolic compliance
entries.text: Strategies, values, policies and governance structures may all exist formally while everyday decisions follow an entirely different logic. Test whether those artefacts meaningfully govern resource allocation, priorities and behaviour.

entries.label: Grounding Failure · the connections between the parts
entries.text: Organisations frequently possess capable functions, talented individuals and substantial resources and still struggle to convert them into collective results. The problem may lie in the quality of the connections between the parts. Strategy must determine how those contributions fit together around the outcome the organisation is trying to create.

entries.label: The people who must make it happen
entries.text: Strategy execution requires more than communicating priorities. People need to understand where the organisation is going, what the larger outcome is, and how their particular contribution connects to it. Without that connection, organisations can generate significant activity while producing fragmented results. Use this with the idea that people sit on both sides of strategy.

entries.label: How we think · same evidence, different conclusions
entries.text: When two groups read the same evidence and reach opposite conclusions, the difference usually sits in the interpretive framework each brings to it. Every strategic assessment is shaped partly by the evidence and partly by the assumptions of the people assessing it. Honest strategy separates the two.

entries.label: How we decide · emotion in the decision
entries.text: Decisions made under emotional pressure can create consequences far beyond the immediate issue. Emotion, group reinforcement and reputational anxiety can drive consequential decisions without sufficient reflection. Separate the presenting problem from the emotional reaction around it and test whether the proposed response is proportionate.

entries.label: How we behave · the gap between intention and action
entries.text: The gap between stated intention and actual behaviour is one of the most revealing leadership diagnostics available. Build accountability into the space between the commitment and the moment of execution, so that what people sincerely intend is what they do when the pressure of circumstances arrives.

entries.label: A disciplined pause
entries.text: Strategy is weakened when leaders become so committed to movement that they ignore capability gaps. A disciplined pause can prevent an expensive failure later. Use this to show System 2 at work.

entries.label: Room to say “We do not yet know”
entries.text: Strong organisations need room to say “We do not yet know” without reading uncertainty as incompetence. That humility improves learning and stops assumptions from hardening prematurely into facts.

entries.label: Knowledge, capability and wisdom
entries.text: Organisations can hold deep technical expertise and still make poor choices when judgement lacks the discipline of purpose. Fragmentation around personalities distorts collective direction. Use this with the six partial readings of the elephant: each expert is accurate about their part.

entries.label: Function and enterprise
entries.text: Finance optimises finance, HR optimises HR, operations optimises operations, and each may perform well individually while the enterprise struggles collectively. Coherence grows when people routinely ask two questions: “What is my function responsible for?” and “What does the organisation need from my function for the whole to succeed?”

entries.label: The person who does not fit the template
entries.text: A team that is too uniform will be blind to the moments it was never built for. When building a team, deliberately include the person who does not fit the template; that person often solves the problem no one else can see.

entries.label: Action-Oriented · overconfidence after a win
entries.text: Overconfidence after a significant victory is one of the most dangerous leadership conditions. Build a habit of consultation that holds regardless of how strong the last result felt.

entries.label: Action-Oriented · committing before counting the cost
entries.text: The leader who promises the board a delivery date in the heat of the meeting, or announces a pricing change before the commercial modelling is done, shows the planning fallacy at work. One discipline: no public commitment to a number, date or outcome above an agreed threshold without a 24-hour pause.

entries.label: Stability · previous success and present discernment
entries.text: Past evidence matters, yet it cannot substitute for present discernment. Organisations need institutional memory without becoming prisoners of historical formulas. What worked before is one input to present thinking.

entries.label: Social · engineered blind spots
entries.text: A leader who fills the room with people who agree has engineered a blind spot and called it harmony. Unwelcome accuracy is worth more than pleasant confirmation. Seek out the person willing to say what the agreeable majority will not, and protect them from the cost honesty usually carries. Use this with Groupthink and Authority.

entries.label: Social · informal pressure
entries.text: Informal social pressure can overpower formally held beliefs. No policy is needed; the presence of particular people is enough to change behaviour. This is culture operating through signals, belonging and perceived approval. Use this with Conformity.

entries.label: Complementary capability
entries.text: Sustainable execution rarely depends on one dominant function. Value is produced when differentiated capabilities are deliberately integrated around a common purpose. Use this with the first point of the three-point check.

entries.label: Where culture is tested
entries.text: Examine the interfaces where culture is actually tested: hand-offs between functions, resource conflicts, decision disagreements and responses to mistakes. These moments reveal whether people experience themselves as contributors to one whole or as representatives protecting separate territories. Use this with the White Space.

entries.label: Invisible walls
entries.text: People can work in the same organisation, attend the same meetings and share the same corporate values while remaining separated by invisible walls: functional silos, hierarchy, professional status, historical conflict or assumptions about whose contribution matters most. Ask the group: what invisible walls are preventing capable people from becoming an integrated organisation?

entries.label: Misallocated Capital · where the resources go
entries.text: Cultures are revealed by their budget allocations and recognition rituals. List the three things the team has invested most resource in over the last quarter and the three things it has most publicly celebrated. If those lists do not match the stated values, the values on the wall are decoration.

entries.label: Strategic Inertia · programmes that outlive their purpose
entries.text: Senior leaders accumulate programmes built to reproduce past breakthroughs. Identify one programme, ritual or initiative that exists mainly because something like it succeeded before, and pull the data on whether it still produces the original effect. If the case for keeping it is mostly nostalgia, schedule its sunset this quarter.

entries.label: Execution Failure · failing, or still maturing
entries.text: Strategic outcomes are usually cumulative. Capability, trust, customer loyalty and operational discipline are built through repeated investments whose effects may not be immediately visible. Good execution distinguishes between an initiative that is failing and one whose results have not yet matured, while using evidence to test whether the underlying assumptions remain valid.

entries.label: Innovation Suppression · protect the truth-teller
entries.text: Organisations often face the most intense resistance to necessary truth from the people who should be most invested in hearing it. Build the protection of truth-tellers into the structure of the culture as well as the values statement.

entries.label: Purpose Drift · small accommodations
entries.text: Drift happens through a series of small accommodations that go unchallenged. What is tolerated becomes what is normal, and by the time the values have shifted no one can point to the moment it happened. Leaders who want to protect what the organisation stands for must challenge early drift.

entries.label: Phase 1 · deciding first
entries.text: Organisations often decide first and then use analysis to validate the decision. Sound strategy needs enough humility to let evidence alter the chosen path. Use this with Confirmation Bias.

entries.label: Phase 1 · diagnosis beneath visible behaviour
entries.text: Organisations misdiagnose problems when they address visible symptoms without examining the beliefs producing them. Persistent silo behaviour or poor accountability may survive new processes because the underlying assumptions remain intact. Ask what is happening, and what logic keeps making this behaviour reasonable to the people practising it.

entries.label: Phases 1 and 2 · disciplined diagnosis
entries.text: Consequential decisions require leaders to separate facts from framing, individual interests from institutional interests, and genuine risk from manufactured urgency.

entries.label: Phase 3 · the sunk-cost trap
entries.text: Organisations often continue weak initiatives because money, reputation or effort has already been invested, defending yesterday’s choice at the expense of tomorrow’s outcome. Sound strategy needs the courage to discontinue an unsuitable course, absorb the immediate cost and return to the principles that should govern the decision.

entries.label: Phase 4 · outcomes taken as proof
entries.text: Senior teams routinely read good outcomes as evidence of sound process. A deal closes or a launch lands, and the messy path that produced it is quietly adopted as the method. Ask participants to pick one recent win and audit how it happened separately from what it produced.

entries.label: Phase 4 · line of sight
entries.text: Leaders have a responsibility to allocate work and to create line of sight between contribution and collective purpose. When people understand where they fit, responsibility becomes more meaningful and coordination becomes easier. Use this with the Phase 4 scanner question.

entries.label: Emotional maturity · alert without becoming absorbed
entries.text: When leaders become psychologically captured by a threat, organisations often inherit that preoccupation through excessive controls, defensive decisions or distorted priorities. Mature leadership keeps problems in proportion and preserves enough internal steadiness to continue exercising judgement.

entries.label: Fear-Dominated · what authority creates
entries.text: A technically correct leader can still generate fear, silence or defensive behaviour through the way they exercise authority. Leaders need to examine what their habitual responses create around them, alongside what their decisions accomplish.

entries.label: Fear-Dominated · anxiety that governs decisions
entries.text: The danger arises when internal anxiety begins governing external decisions. Fear can produce unnecessary control, rushed decisions, avoidance or constant changes in direction.

entries.label: Narcissism-Dominated · the echo chamber
entries.text: When advisers reinforce the posture the leader already wants to adopt, the leadership team becomes an echo chamber. People learn that influence is gained through agreement, and the culture loses the ability to challenge damaging assumptions.

entries.label: Narcissism-Dominated · secure identity
entries.text: Leaders who derive too much identity from position, recognition or being right can experience disagreement as a personal threat. Secure leaders have greater capacity to listen, share authority, acknowledge mistakes and recognise others. Inner security becomes an organisational capability.

entries.label: Grounded Confidence · calm before the crisis
entries.text: In a crisis, organisations with a culture of calm, evidence-based thinking hold their nerve better than those that follow the emotional temperature of the room. Build the capacity for calm assessment before you need it.

entries.label: Psychological Safety
entries.text: Part of an organisation’s culture is what people believe will happen to them if they try something and it fails. Where the prevailing belief is that failure is punished, people stop trying, whatever the stated values say. Examine what people saw happen to the last person who took a risk and got it wrong.

entries.label: Morale Drain
entries.text: Cultures become healthier when people can voice concern, disappointment or uncertainty without being labelled negative or disloyal. Suppressed emotion moves underground.

entries.label: Values Alignment
entries.text: An organisation may repeatedly communicate integrity, collaboration or accountability while rewarding behaviour that contradicts those values. Employees learn that the real culture is encoded in consequences. Culture becomes credible when what leaders praise publicly, tolerate privately and reward materially tells the same story.

entries.label: Listen before you reframe
entries.text: Cultures that move straight from “here is what changed” to “here is what we need you to do next” produce resistance they cannot explain. The resistance signals that people do not yet feel understood. In a restructure, a strategic pivot or a change in leadership, listening is the load-bearing wall. Use this with signals 2 and 6.

entries.label: Emotionally honest leadership
entries.text: Leaders do not strengthen people by pretending that fear, disappointment or grief do not exist. Mature leadership makes space for reality while helping people move from raw emotion toward reflection, meaning and renewed trust. Use this with signal 1.

entries.label: Emotion processed in the right place
entries.text: The leader who has no outlet for genuine emotion carries it into every decision. The leader who processes it appropriately can remain clear-headed in the most emotionally charged situations.

entries.label: Principle 3 · designated challenger
entries.text: Most flawed plans survive because dissent was quietly designed out of the room. Before the next significant decision, invite the one person most likely to disagree and hear them out fully.

entries.label: Verification before response
entries.text: A common and costly strategic failure is acting at the speed of assumption on information that was heard and never confirmed. Build an explicit verification step into decision-making before any significant response.

entries.label: Principle 6 · lessons that change something
entries.text: Review organisational history to recognise the patterns that must be interrupted; recurring problems treated as isolated events return. Reviews create little value when lessons remain conversational. Insight must eventually alter decisions, controls, resource allocation and expected behaviour.

entries.label: From “Me” to “We”
entries.text: A healthy culture creates conditions in which different contributions can genuinely be joined together. This requires a shared identity strong enough to transcend functional identity, relationships strong enough to carry disagreement, and an understanding that no single part can independently produce the whole organisational outcome.

entries.label: Cognitive Integration
entries.text: The most accurate intelligence about what the organisation’s decisions are producing is often held by those furthest from the decision-making centre. Build explicit structures that bring this intelligence from the edges into the rooms where decisions are made.

entries.label: Behavioural Guardrails
entries.text: Leaders who decide by who is loudest in the room, ahead of what is most true in the data, consistently make poor calls. Good judgement goes beneath the surface presentation and the political pressure to what is actually true.

entries.label: Emotional Stabilisation
entries.text: Leadership maturity includes the ability to acknowledge uncertainty without transferring anxiety throughout the organisation. Steadiness means remaining sufficiently grounded to assess reality clearly and respond proportionately.

entries.label: Blind Ideation · Halo Effect
entries.text: Cultures become vulnerable when prestige determines whose ideas matter. Healthy cultures combine competence with humility and value overlooked contributors.

entries.label: Insight from every level
entries.text: Leaders who assume strategic insight belongs only to the senior tier miss what the rest of the organisation sees. The next strategic insight may come from the youngest person on the team.

entries.label: Public Cognitive Humility · self-examination
entries.text: When something goes wrong, positional power makes it easy to locate failure elsewhere: in the team, the environment, the systems or the execution. Ask “Who failed?” and also “What did my decisions, assumptions, signals or omissions make possible?”

entries.label: A common reference point
entries.text: Integration requires a common reference point. When every function interprets priorities primarily through its own objectives, coherence becomes difficult. Shared strategic intent provides the reference against which local decisions can be aligned. Use this in the debrief of the Enterprise Task.

entries.label: C1 · I Know My Biases
entries.text: Leaders need mechanisms that reveal their blind spots as well as their strengths. Acknowledging difficulty deepens trust when it comes with responsibility, learning and perseverance.
